stories.title: COP31 enters extra day of talks amid fears over agreement
stories.summary: There are fears that the COP31 Climate talks in Turkey could end without a deal as a serious dispute over whether even to mention fossil fuels in the final agreement deepens. The talks in Antalya have now into gone into an extra day for negotiations, with the different sides as far apart as ever on fossil fuel inclusion. The draft text on the table this morning is the one issued on Thursday, which dropped all explicit references to fossil fuels. Much of the frustration on the European side comes down to how little it is now asking of the countries opposing it to mention the transition away from fossil fuels. This frustration is being amplified also by the global acceptance now that warming is set to breach the 1.5 degrees Celsius limit set out in the Paris agreement in 2015. In Dubai three years ago, governments agreed to contribute to a global effort to move away from fossil fuels in their energy systems.

stories.title: Why the Deposit Return Scheme is worth keeping
stories.summary: Analysis: While people might not like the plastic bottle and can return scheme, it's a rare example of an environmental policy that we've got right In the latest Climate Change Performance Index Ireland fell four places to 37th out of 64 countries and our performance rating dropped to ‘low’. This independent evaluation of countries collectively responsible for over 90% of global greenhouse gas emissions noted that our progress on climate action is "nowhere near sufficient for ensuring compliance with national and EU commitments". This scathing assessment was published just one week after the Deposit Return Scheme (DRS) for plastic bottles and cans was back in the headlines, following the publication of the accounts of the not-for-profit operator, Re-Turn. Reports that income of €330 million was forecast by 2031 reignited debate about whether the scheme was necessary and fit for purpose. While there are reasonable frustrations about some aspects of the scheme, many of the arguments against it are typical of the delay tactics and "whataboutery" that have stalled and reversed climate progress in Ireland. People might not like the scheme, but it is a rare example of an environmental policy that we’ve got right. Climate action requires behavioural change, but people tend to be subject to status quo bias, where they prefer things to stay the same and dislike change. When policies are proposed or enacted, we often focus on the negatives, such as the inconvenience or costs, rather than the positive impacts of a policy. For this reason, both policy makers and voters prefer 'carrot' climate policies (like subsidies) that incentivise pro-environmental behaviour, rather than 'stick' policies (like taxes) that penalise environmentally damaging behaviour. The problem is that subsidies are less effective than taxes for two main reasons. First, people are typically loss averse, feeling the loss of a tax more than they value the gain of an equivalent amount in the form of a subsidy. Second, taxes signal that a behaviour is undesirable, shifting the social norm as a result.

stories.title: Henry Winkler reveals he was rushed to A+E in Ennis
stories.summary: Happy Days star Henry Winkler has been talking about his eventful week in Ireland which saw him rushed to hospital in Ennis and later hoisted aloft by the Dublin Fire Brigade. The 81-year-old actor, who played Arthur Herbert Fonzarelli aka Fonzie or The Fonz on US sitcom Happy Days from 1974 to 1984, has been touring Ireland with his wife Stacey this week and speaking on Friday's Late Late Show he revealed that he had to visit A+E in Ennis on Thursday. "I want to thank the emergency room doctors and nurses in Ennis," he said. "Yesterday, they took care of me. It was amazing. "I injured myself - I ate too much cheese and I got gout. Don’t eat cheese because I’m telling you, you don’t want this. And then the fire brigade of the city of Dublin took me and put me in their basket and lifted me so I could see the entire city and I soiled myself. It was fantastic." Winkler’s latest Irish trip also saw him visit Kinsale and the Rock of Cashel - where he had the cheese - and he was also spotted in the English Market in Cork and in Kilkenny. The three-time Emmy award winning actor, who is appearing at Comic Con Ireland 2026 at the RDS in Dublin this weekend, has also appeared on tv series Arrested Development and Parks and Recreation and his film credits include Scream in 1996, The Waterboy in 1998, The French Dispatch in 2021 and 2022’s Black Adam.

stories.title: 20 condiments giving Irish cuisine a global flavour
stories.summary: Patrick Hanlon and Russell Alford are freelance food and travel writers who write at gastrogays.com and can be found on social media as @gastrogays From black butter and magic sauces to spice bag seasoning and smoked onion mayo, the Gastro Gays lists Ireland's best condiments. Irish cuisine has long been accused of being bland, boring and unseasoned. Sure, in the past we may not have had access to saffron or chipotle, and baulked at the foreign inclusion of garlic in our lamb stew, but the Irish palate has travelled a long way since then. Spice bags have become the unlikeliest national dish; our fillet rolls are filled with spice-dusted, breaded chicken fillets and slicked in taco sauce; our pizza slices are adorned with spicy pepperoni and drizzled in hot honey. The scale of Irish-made hot sauces alone requires its own entire feature. With the evolution of Irish tastes, our kitchen cupboards are being filled with a dizzying array of international flavours, crafted right here in Ireland. Here are 20 condiments, sauces, sprinkles and marinades tingling Ireland’s tastebuds in 2026.

stories.title: HSE to cut access to knee and hip MRI scans for over-60s
stories.summary: Public health patients over 60 years old will no longer be able to access MRI scans for knee and hip issues under a new cost saving plan by the Health Service Executive (HSE). According to an internal HSE report, seen by RTE News, the Executive is to discontinue hip and knee MRI scans, meaning GPs will no longer be able to refer their patients for the test in a public hospital. The review by the HSE Cost and Productivity Oversight Group outlines how around 21,600 MRI scans are usually carried out in a full year. The report outlines how the HSE relies on private providers for these diagnostics at present and was already €8.1 million over on its budget for medical imaging by the end of September. The move comes as the HSE tries to arrest ballooning budget overruns with Cabinet Ministers on Tuesday signing off on a €780m supplementary budget for the Executive, on top of a €29 billion budget agreed by Government for 2026. The HSE CEO Anne O'Connor insisted on Wednesday that she has made progress in trying to stem budget overspends since she assumed the role earlier this year.

stories.title: Element Pictures makes profit on success of Bugonia film
stories.summary: The main arm of TV and movie production business Element Pictures last year recorded profits of €913,136 on the back of the global box office performance of its dark comedic thriller Bugonia, starring Emma Stone. New accounts for Element Pictures Ltd also show that the firm paid out a dividend of €3.2m last year. The profit of €913,136 for 2025 followed a post tax loss of €315,082 in 2024. The return to profit coincided with Bugonia grossing an estimated $43.8m in global box office takings. Earlier this year, Bugonia was nominated for four Oscars including Best Picture and Best Actress for Emma Stone. The four nominations brought to 30 the total number of Academy Award nominations secured by the Dublin-based production company.

stories.title: O'Leary eyes full-circle glory at National XC champs
stories.summary: Jack O'Leary is hoping for a full-circle moment at the Sport Ireland Campus on Sunday as he bids for his first senior national cross country crown exactly ten years since he won the junior title on the same course. Last year's National Championships saw O'Leary finish in fourth position behind Brian Fay, Nick Griggs and clubmate Cormac Dalton, but three weeks later at the European Cross Country Championships the tables were turned. O'Leary was first Irishman home in fifth position, leading the senior men's team home to a historic silver medal, the first for the country in 25 years. That performance in Lagoa kickstarted a period of success for the Mullingar man. O'Leary has rewritten six of his personal bests in 2026, most recently clocking 1:01.05 for the half marathon to move sixth on the Irish all-time list in his debut over the distance. There was also a top 10 finish at the European Athletics Championships over 10,000m, which rounded out a short but successful season on the track.

stories.title: New Irish short film qualifies for Oscar consideration
stories.summary: Me, Myself and Mary, a new animated short film voiced by Chris O'Dowd and Aisling Bea, has qualified for consideration at the Oscars after being selected by Whoopi Goldberg for the Tribeca Film Festival. The film tells "the true story of how author and journalist Séamas O'Reilly got his days wrong and found himself alone with his boss and the then President of Ireland Mary McAleese while high on drugs". Warning: this film contains bad language and references to drug use Made over seven years by director John Michell and two animators working remotely, producers say the film is a passion project made without funding, public body support or AI. Adapted from a viral social media thread by Derry native O’Reilly (Prestige Drama, Did Ye Hear Mammy Died?), the film recounts the true story of the day he misread his schedule and ended up having "the worse day" of his working life at a function attended by Mary McAleese, President of Ireland from 1997 to 2011. Alongside its Oscar qualification, Me, Myself and Mary has been named a Vimeo Staff Pick and is currently under consideration for both the IFTA and BAFTA Awards.

stories.title: What to know as Dior brings its runway to Dublin in December
stories.summary: The countdown is on for the highly anticipated Pre-Fall 2027 Dior fashion show, which comes to Dublin on 4 December. Ashley McDonnell, Founder of Ireland Fashion Week, joined Today with David McCullagh to talk through the significance of the event. Listen back above. In just two weeks' time, Dublin City will be transformed into an epicentre of luxury fashion, as Derry native Jonathan Anderson, the Creative Director for Dior, brings the fashion house's Pre-Fall 2027 show to the Old Library in Trinity College Dublin. The announcement came amid a swell of global appreciation for Irish fashion talent, from Anderson at Dior, Simone Rocha's beloved label and Sean McGirr's tenure at Alexander Queen. "But it’s been tough at home", McDonnell says. "We didn’t necessarily have the infrastructure or the eco-system or even the talent to help lift these designers up. So they usually have to leave, they have to leave the island to make a name for themselves and to make a career for themselves." She adds that creating that infrastructure was a priority for the Ireland Fashion Week team. "And for them to see someone like Jonathan Anderson rise to the top position in fashion, and bring it back to Ireland, even just in terms of the confidence that it’s going to give people will be huge." Speaking about Anderson's rise to that pinnacle of fashion, McDonnell calls him "a creative genius".

stories.title: EU, UK to spend year brainstorming future ties - Burnham
stories.summary: British Prime Minister Andy Burnham has paved the way for Britain to forge closer ties with the European Union after striking a deal which makes the biggest steps towards the trade bloc than any time since before Brexit. The UK prime minister said the next 12 months would be spent "brainstorming" ideas with the EU for the future relationship between Britain and the bloc. Incremental steps "only take us so far", Mr Burnham said, and suggested the package agreed with Brussels was "probably the limit" of what could be achieved before the next general election. Mr Burnham is expected to set out his view on the options as part of his 10-year plan which will be unveiled in December. Yesterday, he made three significant agreements with the EU in the Belgian capital. A food trading deal, officially known as a sanitary and phytosanitary (SPS) agreement, will end most post-Brexit checks and restrictions on food and agricultural products from March 1, 2028.

stories.title: Bellew Group completes purchase of Solartricity
stories.summary:
Independent electrical wholesalers Bellew Group has announced it has bought solar energy business Solartricity. The Group said its part of its expansion plans in the growing renewable energy market in Ireland. Solartricity was founded in 2014 by Quentin Gargan and delivers energy solutions to customers across the UK and Ireland. The company will continue to operate under its established brand with its management team remaining in place.

The Bellew Group, which has expanded significantly in recent years through growth and acquisitions, now employs more than 300 people. The deal also follows Bellew's recent partnership with technical lighting specialist Element3. The Group described Element3's acquisition as strengthening its capabilities in lighting controls, emergency lighting and lighting distribution, particularly within the data centre market.

stories.title: Irish scrum set for defining test against the Springboks
stories.summary: Given the amount of actions and reactions that can occur when two packs of roughly 900kg each slam together cheek by jowl, it's a near impossible task to referee perfectly. Because of that, your reputation precedes you. When a team or individual is known to be dominant, you will naturally get a few 50/50 calls your way. By the same token, a scrum that struggled last week is also likely to struggle the next week. Sometimes though, there's very little ambiguity to the scrum, and last year's meeting of Ireland and South Africa was the perfect example, as the Springboks minced the Irish setpiece in one of the most dominant scrummaging performances the game has seen. Ireland gave up six scrum penalties to the world champions that evening, with Andrew Porter and Paddy McCarthy both sent to the sin-bin, in addition to the three other cards Ireland picked up that afternoon. However, those numbers don't actually paint a full picture of the dominance, as there were four further penalty advantages from the scrum which were never cashed in – two of which led directly to tries. That was a line in the sand day for Ireland from a scrummaging point of view.

stories.title: Battle lines drawn for Govt over Triple Lock legislation
stories.summary: Taoiseach Micheál Martin has claimed rival parties are putting the lives of Defence Forces personnel at risk by misrepresenting the triple lock legislation facts. Tánaiste Simon Harris has waved the Constitution in the Dáil, insisting "it [Irish neutrality] ain't changing" regardless of any legal developments. The Opposition is united in warning Ireland is facing the biggest threat to our neutrality in a generation. President Catherine Connolly is under pressure to decide between her personal beliefs and her professional role. And a now high-profile but initially dismissed Fianna Fáil backbench amendment, which could yet be the Government's only way of coming through the stand-off unscathed provided Mr Martin commits to a subtle climbdown on his previous views. Since it was first raised in the months leading up to November 2024's General Election, the plan to remove the UN Security Council element of the deeply sensitive Triple Lock legislation has always had the potential to be a debate which divides the country.

stories.title: Oil set for third weekly decline on strong export flows
stories.summary: Oil prices fell today and were set for a weekly decline on strong exports from the Middle East despite Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia's capital Riyadh and reports of tanker disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz. Brent crude futures were down 67 cents, or 0.7%, at $91.31 a barrel this afternoon. US West Texas Intermediate futures for December were down 36 cents, or 0.4%, at $82.85 a barrel, while the more active January contract was down 19 cents, or 0.2%, at $82.85. Brent is on track for a near 5% decline for the week and the December WTI contract for a 6.5% weekly drop as expectations of a supply surplus grew because crude shipments through the Strait of Hormuz have returned to roughly pre-war levels. This would be the benchmarks' third week of decline in a row. "This week we keep having relatively strong export flows out of the Middle East. There is also a narrative ongoing that as long as people are talking, maybe there's a deal in the making," said Aldo Spanjer, commodity strategist at BNP Paribas.

stories.title: South Africa continue to lament Prendergast decision
stories.summary: South Africa assistant coach Mzwandile Stick declared "no one is going to break us" as he backed under-fire head coach Rassie Erasmus and criticised the decision to clear Ireland's Sam Prendergast to play. The 54-year-old, who has requested a full misconduct hearing, plans to host an online watchalong from his team’s Dublin hotel. "He’s been hands-on with our team and we are in a good space," Stick said of Erasmus. "Irrespective of what happened, we love him, we appreciate him and no one is going to break us, I can tell you that for sure. "We’ll be prepared tomorrow. We’re going to make sure we pitch up for our people back at home in South Africa."

stories.summary: Andoni Iraola believes Manchester United have an advantage on Sunday with Mauricio Pochettino set to take charge of his first game but criticised unauthorised drone footage of the Argentinian's first training session. Pochettino faces a daunting maiden outing as boss of the Red Devils on Sunday when they travel to face rivals Liverpool at Anfield. A drone operator has apologised after posting a 12-minute video from Carrington on YouTube – since removed – which Liverpool head coach Iraola admitted he has seen. "Yesterday they were sending me the footage but I think the important part of this is it shouldn’t be legal," said the Spaniard. "It happened to United but it could happen today to me. Yesterday you had access to our training, the cameras recorded also 15, 20 minutes of our training, you know who trained with us, you know who didn’t train. "We know the same but it’s not a matter of the advantage, I think it’s the fact someone can do this. I think there is a reason we train behind closed doors because there are some things you have to respect and I don’t think it’s nice for any club."

stories.title: Preview: War of words tees up fiery Aviva Test
stories.summary: After five days of press conferences and disciplinary hearings, of hip-drops and knee-drops, we have a game to cover. Remarkably, Ireland and South Africa could be doing it all over again next week, depending on how this weekend goes. Popcorn at the ready. If Andy Farrell's side beat the Springboks this evening, and New Zealand and France also win their games with England and Argentina, then it will be Ireland against South Africa once again at Twickenham on Nations Championship finals weekend. A rematch next week could even be on the cards if South Africa win this evening, providing Ireland claim a losing bonus-point, and England get nothing from their meeting with the All Blacks. Winning the Nations Championship would be something major for Andy Farrell's Ireland to use as a World Cup springboard, but with France expected to lock in first place in the northern table this weekend, it looks highly unlikely Ireland will be contesting the overall final on Sunday week in London. A top-two finish in the table would at least guarantee Ireland another Test against either the All Blacks or Springboks next week, and with less than a year to go until the Rugby World Cup, an extra game against top quality opposition would be invaluable to finish off 2026.

stories.title: Ireland XV ease to nine-try victory over Fiji Latui
stories.summary: Ireland XV eased to a nine-try victory over Fijian Latui after a scarcely believable contest at Virgin Media Park. Three yellow cards in five minutes saw Fiji reduced to 12 men for a spell. Thirty seconds after returning to the pitch, Mesake Doge received his second yellow, and Fiji's fourth of the first half, to be sent off. From there, it was a matter of how much Ireland would score as Gus McCarthy and Daniel Ryan finished with two tries each. Paul Boyle was a late withdrawal from the Irish bench due to a neck issue, replaced by Scott Penny. Like the Under-20s in their curtain-raising 31-29 loss to Scotland, the Ireland XV opened the scoring in the fourth minute. Joey Carbery’s line break and delayed pass allowed Connacht talent Ryan to score. The out-half followed that highlight with a total miskick off the tee. Fiji grabbed their only lead in the seventh minute. David McCann robbed a line-out, but Pita Lesivoukionoilau intercepted Fintan Gunne’s pass and was celebrating before reaching the line. Joeli Baleilevuka converted.

stories.title: EU considers tax on big tech companies to fund budget
stories.summary: The European Union is considering a tax on the world's biggest digital companies to fund its next long-term budget, with the measure set to be included in a new spending proposal that is due to be published. That will likely provoke criticism from US President Donald Trump since his administration has reacted angrily to EU fines and moves against Big Tech under its content and competition rules in recent years. EU countries have been discussing the size of the next budget, with Germany leading calls for major cuts after the European Commission last year proposed a two-trillion-euro budget for the 2028-2034 period. Berlin criticised the draft proposal published last month that suggested cutting the bloc's future seven-year budget by €140 billion. EU politicians warned this week that the cuts went too far, setting the stage for difficult negotiations. But even before that, member states must agree among themselves.

stories.title: EU-UK summit: simple messages and complicated politics
stories.summary: Andy Burnham, the great communicator of British politics, had a big-picture story to tell - of lower prices, higher growth and the restoration of the life chances of the young generation. The EU leadership also spoke in big-picture terms - of teaming up for new ventures to promote AI and safeguard the population from malware and malicious actors, and offering glimpses of a route to closer EU-UK relations - warmer, nicer, creating tangible benefits for citizens, not just manufacturers and purveyors of chilled convenience foods. Even if they don't, Council President António Costa assured the British their decisions will be respected, just like the referendum outcome was respected. Lots of smiles and warm words. Keep the communication short and simple. However, somehow a bunch of Eurocrats had contrived to complicate things and leave a bad smell hanging in the air. There was a festering dispute over university fees that - short of firm political intervention by heads of government in the weeks ahead - could sour relations with the British just when things were starting to look good.

stories.title: Govt urged to agree terms of reference for Omagh inquiry
stories.summary: A solicitor representing the families of more than half of those killed in the Omagh bombing has urged the Government to agree the terms of reference for a public inquiry and appoint a chair as soon as possible. Taoiseach Micheál Martin has said he is not contemplating a separate inquiry until a British government inquiry has concluded. Tánaiste Simon Harris yesterday said the Government has not ruled out further action in relation to the bombing, but also said it is important for the UK inquiry to finish first. But the families of those killed say that is not acceptable as it could be several years before the UK inquiry, which is examining whether the attack could have been prevented, publishes its findings. Solicitor John Fox, who represents the families of 16 of the 29 people killed in the bombing in August 1998, has urged the Government to begin the process now. "The families welcome the fact that an Irish inquiry is no longer ruled out, but they heard it through the media, not the Government," he said. "They trust that a formal response and proper engagement will now follow.

stories.title: Man convicted of arson for deadly Palisades fire in LA
stories.summary: A former ride-share driver accused of deliberately setting the blaze that grew into one of the deadliest, most destructive wildfires in Los Angeles history was convicted of federal arson charges in a retrial of the case. Five months after jurors deadlocked in his first trial, a second US District Court jury found Jonathan Rinderknecht, 30, guilty of destroying property by means of fire, and arson affecting interstate commerce in the 2025 Palisades fire. Rinderknecht will be sentenced on 17 March, and First Assistant US Attorney Bill Essayli told reporters that the defendant could face up to 40 years in prison. Prosecutors streamlined their case in the second trial, focusing more on evidence that Rinderknecht was "the only person who could have reasonably, possibly" started the fire and that ruled out other causes, Mr Essayli said. They characterised Rinderknecht, a former Uber driver of US and French citizenship, at both trials as a dejected loner who bore deep resentment against society, particularly the wealthy, and channelled his rage into an act of arson. He was accused of "maliciously" starting a brush fire on 1 January 2025, that was quickly suppressed but smouldered underground for days.

stories.title: Poland condemns Russian airspace 'provocation'
stories.summary: Russia violated Poland's airspace overnight with three objects ⁠that were likely two missiles and a drone, the Polish defence minister has said. The Russian embassy in Warsaw did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Drones have repeatedly strayed into the airspace of countries on NATO's eastern flank since Russia invaded Ukraine in February 2022, fuelling tension with the NATO military alliance and stoking fears that the war could spread. "There has been a violation of Polish airspace and an incursion by objects from the Russian Federation," Defence Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz told a news conference. "There was an Kh-101 missile... In the second case, one can also speak of a missile; in the third, it was most likely a jet-powered drone." The incursions happened as Poland was set to hold military exercises of the 'Coalition of the ‌Willing' of Ukraine's allies.

stories.title: What the EU-UK deal on food means for Ireland
stories.summary: Britain and the EU signed three agreements today that change the terms of the Brexit arrangements. One of those agreements will focus on the cross-border trade of food. Agriculture and Consumer Affairs Correspondent Aengus Cox examines the details. If it goes ahead from 2028, the food and drink agreement between the EU and UK would remove a lot of red tape on animal and plant products that cropped up after Brexit. It would mean British products would need to align with the single market's standards, which would likely be beneficial to Irish producers, as it would level the playing field when competing with their UK counterparts. Though, it's worth bearing in mind that - despite Brexit - the UK is still the single largest destination country for Irish food and drink exports. Latest figures from Bord Bia show that last year that there was a 14% rise in food and drink exports to the UK, reaching €6.7bn. The UK's share of Ireland's overall exports in the sector are steady at 35% (close to where it was just before the UK left the EU).

stories.title: French policemen sentenced for beating black producer
stories.summary: A French court sentenced three police officers to serve time over the beating of a black music producer in 2020, recognising the assault as racist in a rare such ruling in a police brutality case. The assault on Michel Zecler, now 47, triggered renewed outrage in France over police violence, which victims and researchers say is systemic but authorities and law enforcement unions claim is limited to isolated cases. The court sentenced Aurelien Lapersonne, 29, to five years in jail, including three suspended. Philippe Tondeux, 50, was sentenced to five years, including three-and-a-half suspended. Pierre Plantier, 37, was sentenced to five years, four of which were suspended, and was to serve the one year with an ankle tag instead of behind bars. All three officers had apologised to Mr Zecler earlier today, with Plantier in tears.

stories.title: Lee Reeves' funeral told 'his legacy will live on'
stories.summary: The funeral of boxer Lee Reeves has heard that he "touched so many lives" and his "legacy will live on". A large crowd gathered at Our Lady Queen of Peace Church in Limerick for their farewell to the 31-year-old. Members of the Defence Forces, the sporting world, and the wider Limerick community were among those in attendance. Mr Reeves died earlier this week after sustaining injuries in a fight at the 3Arena on 1 August. Dreams by The Cranberries played in the church as his coffin, draped in the Irish tricolour, was carried inside. It had been brought to the church on an adapted gun carriage, as part of the military honours for the service.

stories.title: Ireland drawn to face Croatia in Nations League play-off
stories.summary: The Republic of Ireland have been drawn to face Croatia in their UEFA Nations League promotion/relegation play-off in March. Heimir Hallgrimsson's side were paired with the 2018 World Cup finalists in today's play-off draw in Nyon. Ireland will host the Croatians in the first leg in Dublin on Saturday 27 March. The away leg will be on Tuesday 30 March. Croatia finished third in their League A group, containing England, Spain and Czechia, recording 2-1 home and away wins over the Czechs who were condemned to automatic relegation. Slaven Bilic's side slumped to a humiliating 7-0 defeat at home to England in Rijeka but lost respectably on a 2-1 scoreline in Wembley this month. Ireland's last meeting with Croatia came at Euro 2012, when the latter won 3-1 in Poznan.
